title: Pretraining progress is mostly coming from data
short: Data against model recipes in pretraining, 2019 to 2025
author: Dwarkesh Patel, Jerry Han (Dwarkesh Podcast)
more_note: Its seven Datawrapper charts are worth opening there (hover for every point and its seed spread); this page redraws the four-corner curves and the 7 x 7 grid from those charts' own data and recomputes every multiplier.
takeaway: Training seven yearly open recipes (GPT-2 in 2019 to OLMo-2 in 2025) on seven yearly open corpora (OpenWebText to Ultra-FineWeb) at up to 1e19 FLOPs and scoring on OLMES (ten mostly multiple-choice tasks, at least three seeds per curve), the 2025 corpus matched the 2019 pair's score with 12.0x less compute and the 2025 recipe with 3.7x less; together they saved 15x, a third of the product, though score gains in a one-seed grid are 88% additive.
verdict: Believe the direction at this scale and on this benchmark: the curves reproduce the headline exactly and the corpus explains most of the grid. Read "mostly independent" as true in score points only: in compute the gains overlap (15x together; the 2025 recipe is worth 1.25x on the 2025 corpus), and benchmark leakage or OLMES-tuned corpora could inflate the data side.

headline.k: compute the GPT-2 recipe saves on Ultra-FineWeb instead of OpenWebText, to match the 2019 pair's OLMES score at 1e19 FLOPs
headline.d: 3.7x for the OLMo-2 recipe on OpenWebText; 12.0 / 3.7 = 3.24, the title's ratio

headline.k: OLMo-2 on Ultra-FineWeb against GPT-2 on OpenWebText, the same 1e19 reference (1.57x a year over six years)
headline.d: 12.0 x 3.7 would be 45x: on the 2025 corpus the 2025 recipe adds only 1.25x (recomputed here)
headline.at: Measured jointly, we observe a 1.57x YoY CEG

headline.k: R squared of score = mean + recipe effect + corpus effect on the 7 x 7 grid at 3.16e18 FLOPs, one seed per cell
headline.d: the corpus alone explains 81%, the recipe 7% (recomputed here)

responses.t: Very similar architectures, multiple-choice evaluation, release the checkpoints
responses.n: All seven recipes are dense full-attention transformers (no mixture of experts, "a big multiplier"); multiple-choice scores can be lifted by adding question-answer text, which newer corpora select for; asks for the checkpoints. Patel replied that larger scale may show more and they would try to release checkpoints (none by 27 November).

responses.t: Two confounders: contamination and eval hacking
responses.by: Luca Soldaini (Ai2, OLMo and OLMES), on X
responses.n: Newer corpora may contain benchmark test data, and data recipes are developed against OLMES's own tasks; both would inflate the data gain. No reply found.

responses.t: Use generative perplexity on a stratified held-out set
responses.by: GertLek, with Dwarkesh Patel and Jerry Han, Substack comments
responses.n: Proposes perplexity on a held-out set stratified across corpora; Han: held-out loss chose sizes and checked the recipes, but cannot compare corpora, and a better held-out set "would be really additive".

responses.t: The 2025 corpus has a trained model inside it
responses.by: Nothing Is Accidental, with Jerry Han, Substack comments
responses.n: Ultra-FineWeb is filtered by a trained classifier, so model work sits inside the 12.0x; Han agrees that much data progress is algorithmic filtering, distinct from architecture.

since.n: No code, checkpoints or run tables found on Hugging Face or GitHub (searched 27 November 2026); the only released numbers are the charts' data. The text is unchanged since the Wayback Machine copy of 8 September, 19:10 UTC, apart from how the learning-rate formula is marked up, and the charts' later versions hold the same data.

resources.by: Ho, Besiroglu, Erdil, Owen, 2024 (Epoch AI, third-party)
resources.n: The estimate the post compares itself with: compute to reach a fixed perplexity on WikiText and Penn Treebank halved every 8.4 months (95% CI 4.5 to 14.3) over 2012 to 2023, about 2.7x a year, data quality included.

resources.t: The least understood driver of AI progress
resources.by: Anson Ho, Epoch AI Gradient Updates, 2026-02-25 (third-party)
resources.n: The essay the post starts from: estimates of software progress range from about 1.1x to 300x a year, and much of it may be data quality and a few scale-dependent algorithms. Its table is where the post's "3x per year (95% CI: 1.5x to 64x)" comes from.

resources.t: On the Origin of Algorithmic Progress in AI
resources.by: Gundlach, Fogelson, Lynch, Trisovic et al., 2025 (third-party)
resources.n: The model-side twin of this experiment: ablations of 2012 to 2023 innovations account for under 10x at small scale; most of the rest is scale-dependent (LSTM to Transformer).

resources.t: A Bitter Lesson for Data Filtering
resources.n: The post's evidence that filtering may matter less for large models: with enough compute, the best filter is no filter.

resources.t: Updates, June 2026 (on A Bitter Lesson for Data Filtering)
resources.n: Reads that paper the other way: the compute at which filtering stops paying is far beyond foreseeable budgets, so filtering still pays, especially for small models.

resources.t: DataDecide: How to Predict Best Pretraining Data with Small Experiments
resources.n: The precedent Han cites for ranking corpora by small-model benchmark scores, and how far small-scale rankings transfer.
The evaluation suite: task formats, multiple-choice against cloze scoring, and the ten tasks behind every score here.

resources.t: Architecture research as addressing constraints to scaling
resources.n: The argument the post leans on for why model work matters despite small multipliers: it removes what stops scaling.

kb.n: Owns scaling laws, the 6ND cost and compute-optimal allocation (section 3), which this study's runs use to choose each model size; cites the 12.0x and 3.7x.
Owns what each curation stage buys (section 1 cites this study); the corpora on the data axis are its subjects.
Owns the classifiers behind FineWeb-Edu and Ultra-FineWeb, the two corpora that carry most of the data gain.
